title: The Summer Slump

scenario.situation: July sales came in 15% below June. The business review deck goes out tomorrow.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The VP of Commerce reads the month-over-month drop as evidence the business is contracting and wants to trigger a promo-spend response immediately.
scenario.question: Is Cartwell actually shrinking, or is something else going on?

decisions.prompt: The VP wants a quick answer before the deck goes out. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Confirm the MoM decline
options.detail: Accept the 15% drop as the key fact and look for which channels or SKUs drove it down from June.
options.consequence: You find the decline is broad-based across channels — which makes it look even more alarming. But you've never asked whether June-to-July is normally negative, so you have no baseline to judge against.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the VP's frame and never questioned whether the comparison period was appropriate.

options.label: Benchmark this July against a seasonal baseline
options.detail: Before reading the MoM move as a trend, check whether July routinely underperforms June and compare this July to last July.
options.consequence: You immediately see that July always trails June at Cartwell. The real question shifts to whether this July is better or worse than last July — which is the comparison that removes seasonal noise.

options.label: Survey recent buyers for sentiment
options.detail: Run a quick NPS pulse to see if customer satisfaction dropped in July.
options.consequence: Sentiment is stable — customers aren't unhappy. But this doesn't explain the sales number, and you've spent time on an instrument that wasn't calibrated to diagnose a revenue move.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow, indirect instrument when the answer was already in historical sales data.

options.label: Build a revenue forecast model
options.detail: Fit a trend model to the last 12 months of sales and project whether the business is declining.
options.consequence: The model flags a downward inflection — because you fed it raw monthly data without seasonal adjustment. The model has learned the seasonal pattern as a structural decline.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to modeling before diagnosing — the model inherited the same flawed comparison.

decisions.prompt: You pull monthly revenue data. Which metric do you put in front of the VP?

artifact.title: Cartwell monthly revenue — last 3 months (MoM view)
artifact.caption: Raw monthly revenue. July looks like a sharp drop — but this view contains no seasonal context.

options.label: Month-over-month change (July vs. June)
options.detail: Report the 15% decline from June to July as the primary performance signal.
options.consequence: The chart shows a falling bar, which reinforces the VP's fear. But June is Cartwell's seasonal peak — comparing July to June is like comparing December retail sales to January and calling it a crisis.
options.divergenceCost: Reported a metric that conflates seasonal swing with business trend.

options.label: Year-over-year change (July this year vs. July last year)
options.detail: Compare this July to the same month last year to hold seasonality constant.
options.consequence: Normalized for season, the picture flips: this July is up 8% versus last July. The business isn't shrinking — it's growing, but the MoM lens was hiding it under a predictable seasonal trough.

artifact.title: Cartwell July revenue — year-over-year comparison
artifact.caption: Same month, consecutive years. July this year is up 8% YoY — the seasonal trough is normal; the underlying trend is positive.

decisions.prompt: The YoY view shows +8% growth in July. What do you tell the VP before the deck goes out?

options.label: "The business is growing 8% — no action needed."
options.detail: Declare the business healthy and close the conversation.
options.consequence: You've corrected the VP's frame, but overclaimed certainty. One YoY data point doesn't rule out a genuine slowdown hiding inside the seasonal lift, and you've given no path to monitor it going forward.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed from a single corrected data point and gave the VP no way to track the real trend.

options.label: "MoM overstates the drop because July is seasonally soft — YoY is the cleaner signal and it shows +8%. I'd recommend we track YoY weekly for the next four weeks before deciding on promo spend."
options.detail: Reframe the metric, share the finding, and propose a monitoring path before acting.
options.consequence: The VP understands why the original read was misleading, sees the corrected signal, and has a concrete next step. You've added analytical value without overclaiming — and you've protected the promo budget from a false alarm.

insight: July's 15% month-over-month drop was a seasonal pattern, not a business contraction — comparing to the same month last year revealed +8% growth. The exec's instinct was a plausible but flawed read because month-over-month mixes seasonal swing with underlying trend. The core lesson: always ask whether your comparison period is like-for-like before declaring direction, and hold the causal claim loosely until you have enough YoY observations to confirm the trend.
